methodological_rigor.justification: The study includes a sizable single-center retrospective cohort of 650 women undergoing elective endometrial cancer surgery and defines four analgesia exposure groups, co-primary outcomes, inflammatory markers, and subgroup analyses. The main limitation is nonrandomized analgesia assignment, leaving residual confounding by clinician preference, surgical complexity, ERAS execution, and unmeasured patient factors despite apparently balanced baseline variables. Statistical methods are comparatively strong for an observational study, including prespecified covariates, logistic regression, mixed-effects models for repeated biomarkers, calibration checks, and interaction testing, but there is no propensity-score or instrumental-variable analysis and outcomes are limited to index hospitalization.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective cohort study, giving Oxford LoE 2b. The clinical relevance is high because postoperative analgesia, opioid exposure, PONV, ambulation, flatus, length of stay, and Clavien-Dindo complications are directly relevant perioperative endpoints for endometrial cancer surgery. The translational inflammatory-marker findings are plausible but secondary, and the study does not establish effects on 30-day complications, readmission, quality of life, or long-term oncologic outcomes.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the applicable standard for this observational cohort. The manuscript reports screening exclusions, exposure definitions, co-primary and secondary outcomes, covariates, missingness below 5% in included final models, and statistical model types. Reporting is weakened by the Results section appearing after the Discussion in the normalized manuscript, limited detail on exact group sizes and missing-data handling, no post-discharge follow-up, and no reproducible analytic code or dataset. The figures and tables are described, but the core numerical tables are not included in the normalized text.

novelty_literature.justification: The study offers a meaningful disease-specific extension of multimodal analgesia and ERAS concepts to women undergoing endometrial cancer surgery, comparing opioid-dominant, opioid-sparing, regional, and fully multimodal regimens. The concepts of opioid-sparing analgesia, regional techniques, and inflammatory attenuation are established in perioperative care. Novelty is therefore moderate and lies mainly in the cohort size, four-way real-world comparison, and inclusion of serial NLR and CRP in this cancer-specific setting.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract is structured and quantitatively grounded, and the methods define exposures and outcomes in enough detail to understand the analysis. The manuscript has organizational problems, including a duplicated or misplaced Results section after the Discussion and some repetitive, inflated discussion language. Figure captions are useful for the flow diagram and inflammatory trajectories, but the text sometimes overstates broad implementation and oncologic implications from in-hospital retrospective data.

key_strengths: Large endometrial cancer surgery cohort with clearly defined analgesia exposure groups.
Uses clinically meaningful perioperative outcomes including prolonged length of stay and Clavien-Dindo grade II or higher complications.
Includes adjusted logistic regression and mixed-effects modeling of serial NLR and CRP.
Acknowledges key limitations such as retrospective design, single-center setting, and lack of post-discharge outcomes.
key_concerns: Nonrandomized analgesia selection remains vulnerable to residual confounding despite covariate adjustment.
Outcomes are restricted to index hospitalization, likely missing 30-day complications and readmissions.
The manuscript organization is flawed, with results placed after the discussion in the normalized text.
Claims about immune protection and longer-term oncologic implications exceed the available endpoints.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The study is clinically useful and statistically more developed than many retrospective perioperative cohorts, but it needs major revision for organization, causal framing, and observational bias control. Tier 3 is plausible after those issues are addressed.
